description: About RealPlayRealPlay is a fast-growing Tel Aviv startup in the gaming industry. At the heart of how we operate is a deep understanding of our players, and that depends on clean, trustworthy data. That's where you come in.The RoleRaw data isn't built for thinking with. It's structured for storage: captured efficiently, indexed for retrieval, but shaped for the machine that wrote it, not the person trying to ask questions of it. Turning raw events into something a company can actually reason with takes deliberate work, and that work is what you'll be doing as an Analytics EngineerYou turn raw event logs into clean, well-defined, trustworthy data models: the canonical datasets the rest of the company reasons in. The models you build become the foundation on which everything downstream depends, so a clean foundation makes the next ten analyses faster, the next ten conclusions sharper, the next ten decisions better-grounded. Good analytics compounds on top of good models.The operational framework is engineering discipline applied to analytical artifacts. The models you ship are versioned, reviewed, and tested like production code. Pipelines are observable, so problems surface before consumers find them. Columns are named and documented honestly, because everything downstream (analyses, dashboards, the AI agents querying your data) depends on those names meaning what they say. The deepest form of documentation, though, is the architecture itself: clean models are their own explanation.This work has always mattered, but in an AI-native world, it becomes the most leveraged data work in the company. The ceiling on what an LLM can do with your company's data is set by how clearly that data is modeled. Tangled tables produce confident nonsense; clean, trustworthy ones produce real leverage. The architecture you build is the substrate on which every AI capability (agents, copilots, automated analyses) operates.The role itself has shifted, too. You orchestrate LLMs more than you type line by line. They draft the SQL, the tests, the documentation; you decide what to model, whether the output is trustworthy, and whether the architecture will hold up five models from now. The judgment is yours; the typing is increasingly theirs.In This Role, You WillDesign canonical data models (clear grain, honest names, predictable behavior) that the whole analytics function builds on.Own those models end-to-end: the dbt implementation, the testing, the observability, the SLAs that make them dependable.Evolve the data layer as the product changes, so the architecture stays coherent rather than accumulating legacy.RequirementsWho You Are:You think in first principles. Asked to model active users, you don't reach for the nearest existing query. You ask what active actually means here, who'll use the answer, and what the right grain is. You're suspicious of definitions that haven't been examined.You care about correctness in a way that's almost aesthetic. A column with a misleading name, a model that silently double-counts, a number that looks right but isn't: these bother you the way a typo bothers a careful writer.You take pleasure in things being well-built. A tangled ad-hoc pipeline, an inconsistent naming scheme, a model nobody trusts: they make you want to fix them. You notice when something is well-architected and care about being the person who builds it that way.You think in interfaces. Names are contracts. Grain is a promise. The model you ship today is something other people will build on for years, and you design accordingly.You have engineering hygiene as second nature, or a hunger to develop it. Version control, tests, code review, and observability. You see these as what separates work that compounds from work that has to be redone.You're curious about the business. Understanding what the analytics function is trying to figure out makes you radically better at building the data layer it actually needs.Instrumental Skills & ExperienceThe path from raw events to trusted models runs through specific tools. Experience with the following is useful for this role (though not required):Engineering practices that travel with you regardless of tool: Git, code review, writing tests, and reading other people's code.A version-controlled, tested transformation framework (we use dbt).An instinct for SQL query shape and grain: the picture of right you carry before any query runs. That's what makes judging the LLM's output possible at all.Scripting outside the warehouse for orchestration, custom ingestion, automation (Python or similar).A modern cloud warehouse (we use BigQuery; the patterns transfer).Fluency working with AI coding tools: taste for what to delegate, how to prompt for quality, how to verify the output (Cursor, Copilot, agents). This is how the work happens, daily.

title: Agentic AI Developer

description: The short story is that our agents are now the ones coding and shipping our features. Since the software factory is autonomous, we need an engineer who ensures the pipeline beneath them never breaks.This is a new kind of engineering role - one that exists because AI agents have moved from "experiment" to "production" in modern development teams.Once real work runs through autonomous agents, a new class of problem emerges: they get stuck, lose context, hallucinate about time, drop work silently, or quietly succeed without reporting back.These are not problems you can solve by writing better feature code.We're looking for the person who owns the agents themselves - making sure the multi-agent pipeline that ships our code is reliable, observable, cost-aware, and continuously improving.What we're really looking forWe're not looking for a traditional senior developer. We're looking for someone whose mindset matches a problem that didn't exist 18 months ago.You think in systems, not features.Your instinct on a failure isn't "let me add a try/except" - it's "what monitoring should have caught this 10 minutes earlier?" You see workflows, queues, deadlines, escalation paths.You're deeply skeptical of LLM self-reports.You've worked with language models long enough to know they have no clock, no memory of last Tuesday, and will confidently lie about both. Your default detection signal is filesystem mtime, not asking another model.You're comfortable in the operational layer.Cron jobs, shell scripts, log parsing, subprocess management, REST APIs - these are your daily tools, not exotic territory. Linux is your living room.You write narrow, deterministic code.You resist over-engineering. You prefer a 30-line cron script that does one thing well over a 500-line "monitoring framework." You don't build abstractions for hypothetical future needs.You're a debugger by temperament.Reading raw agent transcripts to figure out what went wrong is interesting to you, not tedious. You'd rather understand a strange failure than work around it.You see prompt engineering as engineering.Rewriting agent behavior is a code change to you - versioned, reviewed, tested in production. Not a side activity.You can be a one-person SRE.You build it, you ship it, you wake up when it breaks. You're comfortable owning a small but critical system end-to-end.Experience we expect• 5+ years writing production software, ideally including time owning systems in production (not just shipping features).• Comfort with Python and Bash at a level where you can write a working watchdog or monitor without looking up syntax. We don't need framework-level expertise - we need fluency.• Hands-on experience with LLM APIs (any major provider). You should have opinions on token costs, caching, context windows, and where models fail in practice.• A background that touches reliability / observability / DevOps / platform engineering. SRE veterans transfer naturally. So do platform engineers and infrastructure folks who've spent time keeping production systems running.• Track record of operational ownership - at least one production system where you were the person who got paged.Bonus• Experience with multi-agent orchestration platforms or autonomous agent frameworks.• Familiarity with workflow tooling (CI/CD, queue systems, distributed cron).• Comfort designing for non-deterministic systems - anything from ML pipelines to flaky distributed systems counts.What makes this role different• You're not on the feature rotation. Building features is what the agents do now. Your tickets are about the agents.• You're early in a new specialty. AgentOps as a discipline is forming right now - the patterns are not yet textbook, and the people doing this work well will define them.• You own your impact metrics. Throughput, stuck-task incidents, cost-per-task - these move directly in response to your work.• You decide what to automate next. Anything humans still do in the loop is fair game.Who this role is not for• People who want to write feature code all day - you won't.• People who think AI agents are a fad - you'll be miserable.• People who need a fully-built playbook - this discipline is still being written.• Pure researchers - this is hands-on engineering, not just paper-reading.

title: Agentic DevOps
location: Ramat Gan, Tel Aviv District, Israel
description: The short story is that we’re building a software factory where autonomous AI agents actually code and ship our features. Since the code is driven by AI, our infrastructure needs to change with it. This is a hybrid DevOps role. Half of the job is what a senior DevOps engineer has always done: keeping cloud infrastructure healthy, deployments smooth, costs sane, and the on-call rotation quiet. The other half is newer and more interesting: supporting a production multi-agent AI pipeline alongside our AgentOps engineer, owning the infrastructure layer beneath autonomous agents that ship our code.You will not be the person tuning prompts or rewriting agent SOUL files - that lives with AgentOps. You will be the person who makes sure the EC2 instances, EKS clusters, Lambda functions, and ArgoCD pipelines that the agents depend on are rock-solid, observable, and ready when they need them.What we're really looking for?We're looking for an infrastructure expert who views Terraform and IaC as a foundation, not the end goal. While keeping our infrastructure-as-code rock solid, you'll spend your time diving deep into system internals, solving complex production bottlenecks, and architectural challenges where DevOps meets AI.You think infrastructure-first.When a production system has a problem, your first questions are about networking, IAM, capacity, deployment state, secrets. You can read a CloudWatch dashboard the way most developers read a stack trace.You're comfortable with both worlds.You can spend the morning debugging an EKS pod that won't schedule and the afternoon helping the AgentOps engineer figure out why a cron job on EC2 is missing its window. Neither feels foreign.You believe in GitOps.Infrastructure is code. Changes go through pull requests. Rollbacks should be a git revert . Manual clicks in a console are an emergency, not a workflow.You're paranoid about blast radius.Before you change a security group, you know exactly what depends on it. Before you redeploy, you know which services will recycle. You think in terms of "what could break, and how do we recover?"You write narrow, deterministic automation.You prefer one well-tested Bash script over a sprawling Python framework. You don't build abstractions for hypothetical future needs. Your YAML is boring on purpose.You're an on-call professional.You've owned production. You know what a good runbook looks like, what a useless alert looks like, and how to write the difference. Quiet pagers are an art form.You're curious about AI infrastructure as a category.You don't need to be an ML engineer, but you find the systems-level challenges of running autonomous agents at scale interesting - the unusual cost shapes, the long-running stateful sessions, the deterministic-vs-probabilistic monitoring problem. You'd want to learn this layer.Experience we expect• 5+ years in DevOps / SRE / platform engineering with hands-on production ownership.• Deep AWS experience - EC2, EKS, Lambda, IAM, VPC networking, CloudWatch, Secrets Manager. You should have opinions on when to use each, and where AWS's defaults will hurt you.• Production Kubernetes, ideally EKS. You can write a Deployment, debug a CrashLoopBackOff, configure HPAs, and reason about resource limits. You understand what kubectl is actually doing under the hood.• GitOps with ArgoCD (or Flux). You've built ArgoCD applications, dealt with sync failures, and know when self-healing is helping vs hiding problems.• Infrastructure as Code - Terraform, CDK, or Pulumi. You've maintained a non-trivial codebase, not just bootstrapped one.• CI/CD pipelines at production scale - GitHub Actions or similar.• Strong Linux and shell skills - cron, systemd, log parsing, subprocess management. Python or Go for tooling beyond shell.• Observability stack experience - Prometheus + Grafana, Datadog, or equivalent. You can build dashboards that engineers actually use, and alerts that don't lie.Bonus• Experience supporting AI / ML production systems (model serving, GPU clusters, batch inference pipelines, vector DBs).• Familiarity with multi-agent orchestration platforms or LLM API ops (rate limits, token cost monitoring, prompt caching).• Experience with Discord / Slack ops integrations - bot infrastructure, webhook reliability, channel monitoring.• Background in cost optimization at the AWS account level.• Fluent in English.What makes this role different• You work with the AgentOps engineer, not under them. You own the infrastructure layer; they own the agent layer. You meet in the middle, and the boundary is collaborative, not territorial.• You're closer to the new stack than most DevOps roles. While other DevOps engineers are still being asked to support traditional microservices, you'll be supporting a production AI pipeline - a category that's still being defined.• Your work is visible. When deployments go smoothly, the agents ship more tickets. When the EKS cluster is healthy, the engineering team forgets about it. Both outcomes are measurable.• You'll shape the playbook. "How do you operate infrastructure for an autonomous agent team" is not a solved problem. You'll write the answer. Who this role is not for• People who want to write only Terraform all day. The job is broader.• People who want to stay away from AI workloads. You'll be supporting one of the most active AI-driven workloads in the company.• People who need a perfectly defined scope. The boundary between DevOps and AgentOps will keep shifting as we learn.• People who prefer enterprise-process environments over pragmatic ownership. We move fast and own outcomes.

Standards)'를 고객에게 매일 우아하고 사려 깊게 전달하는 것입니다. 골드 스탠다드는 리츠칼튼의 근간이며, 매일 우리가 지난 날보다 더 나은 사람이 되도록 인도하는 역할이 되어줍니다. 리츠칼튼을 성공적으로 이끈 문화, 즉 고객 서비스에 대한 토대와 신념을 통해 럭셔리 호스피탈리티 분야의 글로벌 브랜드 리더로서의 명성을 얻었습니다. 우리 팀의 strategy, product, or program leadership, acting as a strategic peer to senior tech executives (CTO/CPO).Deep exposure to cybersecurity, infrastructure, or developer tools, with the technical literacy title: Senior Data Analyst
location: Tel Aviv-Yafo, Tel Aviv District, Israel
description: What's Addressable?Addressable is a Web3 growth SaaS company that operates at the intersection of advertising and blockchain. Our platform helps marketers reach the right audiences by combining on-chain data, social signals, and behavioral intelligence. We enable teams to build targeted audiences, launch effective campaigns, and measure performance across channels.So, what's the job?We're looking for a Senior Data Analyst to join our R&D team and own the advertising data investigation work that powers our platform's targeting and classification capabilities.You'll work with billions of data points across blockchain, social, and behavioral sources - understanding how users behave across different environments, identifying the signals that matter, and translating your findings into classification logic, scoring rules, and algorithms that the platform acts on. Your work directly determines how we identify and reach the right users.This is a full-cycle research role: from hypothesis and experimentation to production validation. The data is messy, the questions are open-ended, and the answers aren't obvious. You'll use SQL and Python as your primary research instruments, alongside modern AI tools (LLMs like Claude, Gemini, etc.) as core parts of your daily workflow - for data exploration, pattern recognition, classification, and accelerating analysis.You will:Own the investigation of large-scale datasets from diverse sources - identify behavioral patterns, surface meaningful signals, and determine what mattersDefine hypotheses about why certain behaviors occur, design experiments to test them, and iterate based on resultsDesign and own classification logic, scoring rules, and segmentation approaches using SQL, Python, and AI-assisted toolingUse LLMs and AI tools as core parts of your workflow - for data exploration, classification, labeling, and enrichmentEvaluate new data sources and determine whether they improve classification quality and accuracyDrive the translation of your findings into production-ready rules and algorithms, working closely with researchers and engineersRequirements:Sounds great! Am I the right fit?You'll likely be a strong fit if you have:~5 years of experience in data analysis, research, or a related analytical roleStrong SQL skills and experience working with large datasets (Spark, Athena, BigQuery, or similar)Proficiency in Python for data exploration, scripting, and automationA hypothesis-driven mindset with strong statistical thinking - you naturally ask “why is this happening?”, design experiments to find out, and know when a result is meaningful vs. noiseComfort using AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, etc.) to enhance and accelerate your analytical workCuriosity and a self-driven approach to research - you work independently, structure your own approach to ambiguous problems, and drive work forward without waiting for directionInterest in or familiarity with ad tech, programmatic advertising, or audience targetingStrongest candidates will have:Experience in ad tech, programmatic advertising, or performance marketingFamiliarity with audience targeting, attribution, behavioral data, or identity resolutionExperience with DSPs, DMPs, ad exchanges, or related programmatic infrastructureExperience building rules, scoring logic, or classification systems that a product or platform acts on - not just analysis that people readExperience using LLMs for data classification, labeling, or enrichment tasks at scaleWhat Success Looks LikeThe classification logic and rules you build are validated against real outcomes and adopted into production.You test hypotheses systematically, explain what worked and why, and shape the research agenda - not just execute on it.Researchers and engineers trust your findings and build on them.

description: Grab your cape, become a SuperHyro!Hyro, the leader in Responsible AI Agents for Healthcare, enables health systems to safely automate workflows and conversations across their most valuable platforms, services, and channels - including call centers, websites, SMS, mobile apps, and more. not just charts.Exceptional English communication skills, both written and spoken, for clear collaboration with PMs, engineers, customers, and leadership.Strategic mindset with the ability to translate vague business challenges into structured analytical plans.Bonus PointsExperience with NLP or conversational data, including intent analysis and defining quality metrics for model evaluation.Proficiency in Python for analysis and experience scaling data processes within high-growth, evolving infrastructure.Previous experience in the healthcare industry or working with highly regulated data environments.Equal Opportunities:Hyro is an equal opportunity employer.
